newsitem.title: PUERTO RICO: Puerto Rico governor makes case for U.S. statehood.
newsitem.headline: Puerto Rico governor makes case for U.S. statehood.

text.p: For Puerto Rico Gov. Pedro Rossello, whether the U.S. territory should become a state is a simple matter of democracy and citizenship, not culture or sovereignty.

"For me this is a question of rights, of democratic rights or civil rights," he said in an interview this week. "It's a question that should be asked in the context of whether we in Puerto Rico want to be American citizens or not, and if you answer in the affirmative, then for me the only option is really full participation, with your full citizenship rights, privileges and responsibilities."

Puerto Rico, an island of 3.7 million about 1,000 miles (1610 km) southeast of Miami, has been a U.S. possession for 99 years, since Spain ceded it to the United States after the Spanish-American War. Its residents became U.S. citizens in 1917 and Puerto Rico became a U.S. commonwealth in 1952.

The question of its status has raged since 1898, at times violently, with residents heatedly debating whether Puerto Rico should become a state, seek independence or remain a commonwealth, with close U.S. ties, freedom from federal taxes and perks of nationhood such as its own Olympic team.

The debate has burned brightly in recent months. In November, Rossello, leader of the pro-statehood New Progressive Party (NPP), won re-election with 51 percent of votes cast, the first absolute majority ever won by an NPP governor. The NPP also won overwhelming majorities in the legislature, which statehood advocates called a mandate that the island end its second-class status.
"If ... Puerto Rico wants to maintain its American citizenship, then it makes no sense to have that citizenship only in a limited fashion," Rossello said.
Public opinion polls have shown that 95 percent of Puerto Ricans want to remain U.S. citizens.

Island residents enjoy one of the highest standards of living in Latin America, although per capita income is half of that in Mississippi, the poorest U.S. state. They move freely between Puerto Rico and the mainland -- some 2.4 million Puerto Ricans live in the 50 states.
But island residents do not vote in presidential elections, have only a non-voting representative in Congress and limited federal benefits.

Skeptics question how much opinion on the island could have changed since a 1993 plebiscite, when 48 percent of Puerto Rican voters chose commonwealth status, 46 said they supported statehood and the remainder chose independence.
But Rossello said the terms of commonwealth status proposed by the opposition Popular Democratic Party (PDP) were unrealistic in 1993.

For example, he said a provision of commonwealth status voted on in 1993 was for Puerto Rico to have full participation in federal programs, but not pay federal taxes. "As Congress enters the process, it would be defining options that are valid under the U.S. Constitution," he said.

Skeptics also question whether Puerto Rico could win support for statehood in Congress when so many members of the Republican majority have been opposed to the use of the Spanish language in U.S. public life.

Rossello acknowledged that "there are some constituencies that maybe feel threatened by the increasing influence of the Spanish-American citizen." But he argued that middle America could be sold on statehood for Puerto Rico, that the island could be an asset to the nation, particularly with the growing importance to U.S. business of Latin America markets.
"Puerto Rico represents, again because of its characteristics, something that's positive in the economic environment that's developing in the Americas," he said.

U.S. Rep. Don Young, R-Alaska, has said he plans to re-introduce a bill that received some support in Congress last year that would call for a binding plebiscite next year, with a phase-in to carry out the option chosen in 10 years.
President Bill Clinton also wrote to Rossello this month and said he would work to resolve Puerto Rico's status.
